subject: Anthropology
title: Control of Fire
description: A quick, practical guide to Control of Fire.

hook.text: Raw meat takes hours to chew. Cooked meat takes minutes. Fire didn't just warm us — it changed our bodies.

buildup.text: Evidence of controlled fire use dates to at least 400,000 years ago, though earlier hints exist at 1.5 million years.

discovery.text: Cooking breaks down food, releasing more calories. This fueled bigger brains and allowed smaller guts and teeth.

twist.text: Fire also created social space. Gathering around flames at night built bonds, storytelling, and group identity.

climax.text: Fire transformed diet, anatomy, and social life. Richard Wrangham calls it the spark that made us human.

punchline.text: Cooking made us who we are.

quiz.question: How did fire affect human evolution?
options: Cooking allowed bigger brains and smaller guts
It was only used for defense

details.summary: Control of fire was a transformative milestone in human evolution, enabling cooking, warmth in cold climates, protection from predators, and social gathering around hearths. Evidence suggests occasional fire use by 1.5 million years ago, with habitual control established by 400,000 years ago.
details.whyItMatters: Fire transformed human biology and culture. Cooking made more calories available from food, potentially fueling brain expansion. Fire extended the day for social interaction, provided defense against predators.
takeaways: Fire was controlled occasionally by 1.5 million years ago
Cooking made more calories available, possibly fueling brain growth
Fire enabled warmth, protection, and extended social time

faq.question: Did cooking drive human brain evolution?
faq.answer: Richard Wrangham's cooking hypothesis argues that cooking softens food and increases caloric extraction, providing the energy surplus needed for brain expansion. This remains debated — the timeline of fire control does not perfectly match brain expansion — but cooking clearly became essential to.

faq.question: How do we know when hominins first controlled fire?
faq.answer: Evidence includes charred bones and plant material, ash layers, burned stone tools, and hearth structures in archaeological sites. Early evidence is ambiguous — natural fires could produce similar traces.
